title: Faith in place
author: Sean Harris
summary: Sean Harris adapts a short talk he gave at his church into a reflection for anyone serving people and places, whether motivated by faith or a line manager. Using the road-safety mantra Stop, Look, Listen, he offers three invitations. Stop means resisting the rush to respond with more activity, more funding and more reports, and asking what is stopping families and children from taking part. Look means noticing who is missing, who is already doing the work, and valuing lived experience as much as professional expertise, illustrated by a Citizens UK campaign on public transport harassment. Listen means deep social listening that turns into change, as in the Real Living Wage campaign that began in East London in 2001 and now covers over 16,000 employers. He closes with Gaudi's line that his client was not in a hurry and with the difference between building a monument and leaving a legacy.
points: More activity does not automatically produce more progress, so stopping to understand the problem before choosing a solution creates room for better questions.
Looking carefully means asking whose voices are absent and who is already doing the work, rather than arriving with a shiny new initiative and a logo.
Organisations in schools and charities can become so good at describing needs that they overlook the knowledge and capacity for change within the communities they serve.
Deep social listening only matters if it creates deep social change, as the Real Living Wage campaign shows with 16,000 employers and over 4 billion pounds for low-paid workers.
The Gaudi story frames the leadership choice between a monument that says look what I built and a legacy that asks what others can build upon.
quotes: I am increasingly of the belief that more activity doesn’t automatically translate to more progress or impact.

Stopping creates space to ask better questions. In my case, as somebody obsessed with research, data and learning, the act of stopping also gives me chance to consider what I already know and what I might be missing.

We, especially in schools and charities, can become so accomplished at describing people’s needs that we forget to recognise the knowledge, aspirations and capacity to shape change that exists in the places we serve.

I am also aware that we are not short of reports telling us what’s wrong with places. I suspect we could build a reasonably substantial extension to most public buildings using the weight of published reports about poverty alone.
Rather than somebody deciding what needed to happen for them, those affected were involved in determining what needed to change with them.
A commitment to deep social justice requires a commitment to deep social listening. But, deep social listening must create opportunities for deep social change and must be implemented carefully.
A monument says, “Look what I built.” But a legacy asks, “What did I leave for others to build upon?
